title: Human Impact on Environment
summary: Environmental problems arise from natural disasters and from human activities; a disaster causes large-scale damage to life and property, locally or globally. Nature can recover from natural events, but a growing human population and careless use of resources degrade and pollute the environment. Government agencies give early warnings: the India Meteorological Department (cyclones, heat and cold waves), INCOIS Hyderabad (tsunami), the Central Water Commission (floods) and the Geological Survey of India (landslides). The disaster helpline is 1070.

Floods occur when heavy monsoon rain exceeds the capacity of river banks or drainage is poor; humans make them worse by blocking natural flow. They destroy life, crops, houses and roads and can spread epidemics (drink boiled water, eat cooked food), though they also enrich the soil. Prevention: no building on river beds; timely desilting of channels and reservoirs; building public structures above past flood levels; flood-proof buildings; ready evacuation plans and centres. Cyclones are intense low-pressure storms that hit India's coasts, especially the Bay of Bengal (Odisha super-cyclone, 1999), in April–May and October–December. Precautions: cyclone-safe buildings, removal of weak trees and unsafe structures, storing food, water and lights, moving to shelters, ignoring rumours, and inoculation after the storm.

An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the earth's crust when rocks give way to forces inside the earth (Latur 1993, Bhuj 2001, Sikkim 2011). Its intensity is recorded by a seismograph and expressed on the Richter scale (C.F. Richter): up to 3 causes no damage, above 8 brings buildings down. Most harm comes from falling objects and collapsing buildings. Safety: earthquake-resistant buildings; during a quake take cover under a strong table or bed, protect the head, keep away from glass, windows and heavy furniture, stay on the same floor and never use a lift; outdoors move to an open space; afterwards expect aftershocks and keep away from beaches. A tsunami ('harbour wave', Japanese) is a huge displacement of sea water caused by an earthquake under the ocean (or landslides and volcanoes) — Indian Ocean tsunami 2004, Japan 2011 with the Fukushima nuclear leak. Coastal tree cover reduces its effect.

Forest fires are caused by lightning striking dry trees, by heat built up in dry litter in summer and the dry season, and by human negligence (lighted matches, cigarettes). They destroy timber, biodiversity and livelihoods, cause soil erosion and add to global warming. Control: remove dry litter in summer, dig fire lines, call the fire brigade, never leave fires burning in forests. A landslide is the downhill movement of rock, earth or debris when a slope becomes unstable — triggered mostly by heavy rain, and by earthquakes and erosion, and made worse by deforestation, blasting and construction; it is a hazard in hills, steep river banks and coasts. A cloudburst is extreme rain in a few minutes, causing flash floods and landslides (Leh, 2010).

A large population needs more land, water, food, energy and housing, leading to deforestation, pollution, depletion of fossil fuels, biomagnification, ozone depletion, global warming and waste. Deforestation (cutting forests for farming, grazing, wood, paper and building) destroys habitats and biodiversity, reduces rainfall, lowers the water table, causes soil erosion and desertification and raises CO₂. Remedies: laws against felling, reforestation (replanting where forests were removed), afforestation (new forests on land that was not forest), Van Mahotsav (planting in the first week of July), silviculture (growing forest trees) and social forestry. In the Chipko movement, women of the Himalayan region hugged trees to save them.

Pollution is an undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, water or land that harms life and property. Air pollution comes from vehicles, industries and burning fuels — CO, SO₂, nitrogen oxides, suspended particulate matter (SPM) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Primary pollutants are released directly (CO, SO₂, NO, SPM); secondary pollutants form in the air from them (ozone, PAN, acids). Water pollutants include infectious agents from excreta, pesticides, detergents and oil, fertilisers, acids and metals from industry, radioactive materials, and heat from power plants. Soil pollution comes from plastics and household waste, industrial waste and excess agrochemicals. Noise (unwanted sound, measured in decibels) causes hearing loss, headache, high blood pressure and lack of sleep; control it by low volumes, silencers, limiting horns and loudspeakers, and green belts.

Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off and sewage enrich water with nitrates and phosphates; algae grow rapidly (algal bloom), then die and decompose, using up the dissolved oxygen, so fish and other animals die. Biomagnification: non-biodegradable chemicals such as DDT enter a food chain in small amounts and become more concentrated at each trophic level — water 0.2 ppm → algae 77 ppm → fish 500–600 ppm → pelican 1700 ppm. In fish-eating birds this caused thin egg shells that broke, so their populations fell.

Biodegradable waste (leaves, dung, food, paper) is broken down by microbes; non-biodegradable waste (plastics, glass, aluminium cans, batteries, e-waste, DDT) does not decompose easily and builds up in the environment. Open dumps breed flies, rats and mosquitoes and pollute water. Landfills and incineration (which releases toxic gases) are used, but the best way is to produce less waste — the 4 Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Repair, Recycle (paper and plastic recycling, compost, biogas from dung).

Ozone depletion: the ozone layer blocks the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) from refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays release chlorine, which breaks ozone (O₃) into oxygen, thinning it by 30–40% over the Arctic and Antarctic (the 'ozone hole'); more UV causes sunburn, skin cancer, cataract, genetic damage and lower productivity — so people near the poles suffer more skin cancer. Ozone depletion is a human-made, not a natural, disaster. Global warming (greenhouse effect): CO₂, methane and N₂O let sunlight in but trap the heat radiated back; deforestation and fossil fuels have raised the earth's temperature by about 1 °C in 100 years, melting glaciers, raising sea levels (threatening low islands such as the Maldives), making weather unpredictable, reducing crop yields and disturbing fish breeding.

Photochemical smog forms when sunlight acts on nitrogen oxides, hydrocarbons, SO₂ and soot in stagnant air, producing ozone and PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate) that irritate the lungs and eyes and harm crops. It is held near the ground by thermal (temperature) inversion — a layer of cool air at the ground trapped under a layer of warm stagnant air, so pollutants cannot rise. Acid rain forms when SO₂ and nitrogen oxides react with water in the air to form acids; it kills fish (below pH 4.5), damages forests, soil and crops, corrodes metals and erodes marble monuments such as the Taj Mahal.

objective: Fill in the blanks: (a) The biggest source of nitrogen is ________. (b) A tsunami is caused by ________ under the ocean.
Write True (T) or False (F): (a) Ozone depletion is a natural disaster. (b) Heterotrophs are called decomposers.
(a) False — it is caused by human use of CFCs. (b) False — decomposers (saprotrophs) are one kind of heterotroph; heterotrophs are consumers.
Write True (T) or False (F): (a) Forest fires are caused by heat in litter during the rainy season. (b) Landslides are a hazard in hills, steep river banks and coasts.
(a) False — this happens in summer and the dry season. (b) True

case.passage: Farmers near a lake used large amounts of fertilisers and sprayed DDT on their crops. Rain washed the chemicals into the lake. Soon the lake was covered with a thick green layer of algae, and later many fish died. Scientists found that DDT was 0.2 ppm in the lake water but 1700 ppm in the fish-eating pelicans, whose eggs had very thin shells.

vsa: Name the scale used to measure the intensity of earthquakes and give three precautions during an earthquake.

Richter scale. Precautions: take cover under a strong table or bed and protect your head; keep away from glass windows, heavy furniture and electric poles; do not use lifts — stay on the same floor or move to an open space.

vsa.note: April 2019 also asked the cause of an earthquake: the sudden release of energy when rocks inside the earth give way.

vsa: Write four steps to prevent damage due to floods.
No construction on river beds; timely desilting of drains and reservoirs; building houses and public buildings above past flood levels (flood-proof buildings); a ready evacuation plan and centre.
Name two major water pollutants and their sources.
Fertilisers and pesticides (agricultural run-off); sewage with disease-causing microbes (human and animal excreta); industrial waste such as acids and heavy metals (factories).
What is biomagnification? Explain with a food chain.
The increase in the concentration of a non-biodegradable chemical such as DDT at each higher level of a food chain. Water (0.2 ppm) → algae (77 ppm) → fish (500–600 ppm) → pelican (1700 ppm).
Differentiate between biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste with examples.

Biodegradable waste is broken down by microbes into harmless substances (vegetable peels, paper, dung). Non-biodegradable waste is not broken down easily and stays in the environment (plastic, glass, aluminium cans, DDT).
What is the ozone hole? Name the chemicals responsible.

The thinning of the ozone layer, especially over the Arctic and Antarctic, letting more UV rays reach the earth. It is caused by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) from refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays.
sa: Write three serious consequences of the rise in global temperature in the last 100 years.

Any three: melting of glaciers and ice caps and rise in sea level; submerging of low coastal areas and islands such as the Maldives; unpredictable weather; early maturing of crops with smaller grains and low yields; disturbed hatching of fish eggs.

sa.note: October 2016 also asked what global warming means and its causes — rising average temperature of the earth due to greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) released by burning fossil fuels and deforestation.

sa: Write three broad causes of forest fires.

(1) Natural causes such as lightning striking dry trees. (2) Heat built up in dry litter and biomass in summer and the dry season. (3) Human negligence — carelessly dropped lighted matches, cigarettes or bidis, or burning wood left behind.
What is biomagnification? How did DDT reduce the population of pelican birds?

Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of a non-biodegradable chemical at each higher trophic level. DDT sprayed on crops reached the water (0.2 ppm) and passed through algae and fish into pelicans (1700 ppm). The high DDT in the birds made their egg shells thin, so the eggs broke before hatching and the population fell.
What are primary and secondary air pollutants? Give examples and describe two major primary pollutants.

Primary pollutants are released directly into the air (CO, SO₂, NO, SPM); secondary pollutants form in the air by reactions of primary pollutants (ozone, PAN, sulphuric acid). Carbon monoxide — from vehicle exhaust and incomplete burning; it combines with haemoglobin and reduces oxygen supply. Sulphur dioxide — from burning coal and oil; it irritates the lungs and causes acid rain.

sa.note: October 2016 asked why VOCs and SPM are air pollutants: they come from vehicles, industries and burning fuels and cause breathing problems, smog and lung disease.

sa: What is eutrophication? Write the sequence of events that kills aquatic animals.

Eutrophication is the enrichment of a water body with nutrients (nitrates and phosphates) from fertilisers and sewage. Sequence: nutrients reach the water → rapid growth of algae (algal bloom) → algae die → bacteria decompose them, using up dissolved oxygen → fish and other animals die from lack of oxygen.
la: Explain eutrophication and biomagnification and their role in water pollution.

Eutrophication: run-off of fertilisers and sewage adds nitrates and phosphates to lakes and ponds, causing an algal bloom; the algae die and are decomposed by bacteria, which use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish and other aquatic animals die and the water becomes foul. Biomagnification: non-biodegradable pesticides like DDT washed into water are taken up by algae and pass along the food chain, becoming more concentrated at each level (water 0.2 ppm → algae → fish → birds 1700 ppm); top consumers suffer, e.g. birds lay thin-shelled eggs. Both make water unfit for life and show how farm chemicals pollute water.
What is global warming? Explain its causes, why it is a global problem, two other global environmental problems, and four consequences.

Global warming is the rise in the average temperature of the earth. Causes: greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, N₂O) from burning fossil fuels, industries, vehicles and deforestation trap the heat radiated by the earth (greenhouse effect). It is global because gases released anywhere spread through the whole atmosphere and affect all countries. Other global problems: ozone depletion and acid rain (also photochemical smog). Consequences: melting glaciers and rising sea level; flooding of low coasts and islands; unpredictable weather and more extreme events; lower crop yields; disturbed breeding of fish and other animals.
Describe the causes, effects and prevention of deforestation.

Causes: clearing forests for agriculture, grazing, housing, roads and industry, and for wood and paper. Effects: loss of habitat and biodiversity; reduced rainfall and a lower water table; soil erosion and desertification; more CO₂ and global warming; floods and landslides. Prevention: laws against felling; reforestation and afforestation; Van Mahotsav planting; silviculture and social forestry; people's movements like Chipko; using less paper and wood.
What is an earthquake? How is its intensity measured? Describe the safety steps before, during and after an earthquake.

An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the earth's crust caused by the release of energy when rocks inside the earth give way. Its intensity is recorded by a seismograph and expressed on the Richter scale. Before: build earthquake-resistant structures and keep an emergency kit. During: take cover under a strong table or bed, protect the head, keep away from glass and heavy objects, do not use lifts, and outdoors move to open ground away from buildings, trees and wires. After: keep calm and follow radio instructions, expect aftershocks, keep away from beaches, clean up spilled flammable liquids, give first aid and inform rescue teams about trapped people.
